knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

```{r library}
library(decisions)
```

## Overview

Different providers host different decision models. The decisions package
gives them one interface. So you can run the same question with each model and
compare the results.

This vignette compares three models on one text task:

* Jev, from TypeSafe, with `decider_typesafe()`.
* Microsoft-Decision-1, through OpenRouter, with `decider_openrouter()`.
* The Decisions API of OpenAI, with `decider_openai()`. Its default model is
  `gpt-6-luna`.

The results below come from live calls. The package saved them in
`inst/extdata`, so this vignette builds without a key and without a network.
The code that made them is in `data-raw/vignette_results.R`.

## Credentials

Each provider has its own key. `decide()` reads the key from an environment
variable when it sends the requests, as ellmer does.

| Provider | Decider | Environment variable |
|---|---|---|
| TypeSafe | `decider_typesafe()` | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` |
| OpenRouter | `decider_openrouter()` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| OpenAI | `decider_openai()` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |

Set the variables in `~/.Renviron`, then restart R. A decider holds no key.
Each decider also takes a `credentials` function that returns the key. The
function replaces the environment variable.

## Data

The package has the dataset `ohio_injuries`. It has the narratives of 464
severe work injuries in Ohio. The source is the Severe Injury Reports of the
U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), with the filters
Year 2025 and State Ohio (<https://www.osha.gov/severeinjury>). The
column `collapsed_nature_title` has five injury types: `amputation`,
`fracture`, `crushing injury`, `thermal burn` and `concussion`. See
`?ohio_injuries` for the details.

For context: the NIOSH Center for Workers' Compensation Studies reports the
claim counts and rates of the Ohio Bureau of Workers' Compensation
(<https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/worker-comp/about/index.html>).

The five groups differ in size: 187 amputations and 242 fractures, but only 14
crushing injuries, 15 thermal burns and 6 concussions. We take all the reports
of the three small groups and 20 reports of each large group. The seed is
fixed. This gives 75 narratives.

```{r injuries, script = TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
injuries <- ohio_injuries |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(n = 20, by = collapsed_nature_title)

dplyr::count(injuries, collapsed_nature_title)
```

```{r saved, echo = FALSE}
saved <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "choosing-a-model.rds", package = "decisions"))
stopifnot(identical(injuries$id, saved$injuries$id))
```

The truth is the column `collapsed_nature_title`, a factor. Its levels are the
five injury types, in the order above.

## Question

One choice question has the five injury types as its answers. The descriptions
are general. The model reads the narrative of each report.

```{r question, script = TRUE}
nature <- question_choice(
  "Which injury does this report of a work injury describe? Choose the main injury.",
  c(
    amputation = "A body part is cut or torn off, in whole or in part.",
    fracture = "A bone is broken or cracked.",
    `crushing injury` = "A body part is squeezed hard between objects, and the tissue is damaged.",
    `thermal burn` = "Heat, flame, hot liquid or a hot surface burns the skin.",
    concussion = "A blow or a shake to the head hurts the brain."
  )
)
```

## Three models

`purrr::map()` runs `decide()` once for each decider. One call of `decide()`
uses one model. The list `deciders` is named, so the list of answers is
named too.

```{r decide, eval = FALSE, script = TRUE}
deciders <- list(
  jev = decider_typesafe(),
  microsoft = decider_openrouter("microsoft/microsoft-decision-1"),
  openai = decider_openai()
)

answers <- purrr::map(deciders, \(decider) decide(decider, nature, text = injuries$final_narrative))
```

```{r show-decide, echo = FALSE}
answers <- saved$answers
```

Each element of `answers` is a tibble with 75 rows, in the order of the
narratives. We bind the three tibbles and add the truth.

```{r results, script = TRUE}
results <- answers |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "model") |>
  dplyr::mutate(truth = rep(injuries$collapsed_nature_title, times = length(answers)))
```

The levels of `.pred_class` are the five answers, as in `truth`. A name with a
space gives a probability column with a clean name: `crushing injury` gives
`.pred_crushing_injury`.

```{r columns, script = TRUE}
grep("^\\.pred_", names(results), value = TRUE)
```

## Performance

yardstick reads the columns that `decide()` returns. `accuracy()` compares
`truth` with `.pred_class`. `roc_auc()` takes the five probability columns, in
the order of the levels of `truth`. With more than two classes, it computes the
multiclass ROC AUC of Hand and Till.

```{r performance, script = TRUE}
metrics <- yardstick::metric_set(yardstick::accuracy, yardstick::roc_auc)

results |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  metrics(
    truth,
    .pred_amputation, .pred_fracture, .pred_crushing_injury, .pred_thermal_burn, .pred_concussion,
    estimate = .pred_class
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(model, .metric, .estimate)
```

A row with an error has `NA` answers, and yardstick removes it. The table shows
how many rows each model answered.

```{r errors, script = TRUE}
results |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(rows = dplyr::n(), errors = sum(!is.na(.error)))
```

The confusion matrix of each model shows the counts. The rows are the answers
of the model, and the columns are the truth.

```{r confusion, script = TRUE}
results |>
  split(results$model) |>
  purrr::map(\(x) yardstick::conf_mat(x, truth, .pred_class)$table)
```

All three models do well on this task, and their scores differ by a few
reports. Seventy-five narratives and small groups give a rough comparison only. The
group `concussion` has 6 reports, so one report changes its share by 17
points. Use more rows before you choose a model for real work.

## Cost and time

Each provider reports different things. OpenRouter reports the cost of each
call. TypeSafe and OpenAI report none, so `.cost` is `NA` for them, and
`decide()` prints one message about it. All three report the input tokens.
`.seconds` is the time of one response. The requests run in parallel, so these
times do not add up to the time of the whole call.

```{r cost, script = TRUE}
results |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    input_tokens = sum(.input_tokens, na.rm = TRUE),
    cost_usd = if (all(is.na(.cost))) NA_real_ else sum(.cost, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_seconds = median(.seconds, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

The prices of the providers differ. To compare the cost, take the input tokens
and the price list of each provider.
